title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: The princess sat in her armchair, silent and smiling; the prince sat down beside her. Kitty stood by her father's chair, still holding his hand. No one spoke.
It was the princess who first put everything into words, translating thoughts and feelings into practical questions. And to all of them, for the first minute, that felt strange and almost painful.
"When is it to be? We have to arrange the blessing and the announcement. And when will the wedding be? What do you say, Alexander?"
"There he is," said the old prince, gesturing toward Levin. "He's the chief person in this business."
"When?" said Levin, blushing. "Tomorrow. If you ask me, the blessing today and the wedding tomorrow."
"Come now, _mon cher_, don't be absurd!"
"Well — in a week, then."
"He's out of his mind."
"No — why is that?"
"Well, I never!" said the mother, smiling, pleased by his eagerness. "And what about the trousseau?"

"Will there really have to be a trousseau and all the rest of it?" Levin thought, horrified. "But can a trousseau and a blessing and all that — can any of it spoil my happiness? Nothing can spoil it." He glanced at Kitty and saw that she was not in the least, not in the slightest, troubled by the question of the trousseau. "Then it must be all right," he thought.
"I don't know anything about it; I was only saying what I'd like," he said apologetically.
"We'll talk it through, then. The blessing and the announcement can happen now. That's very good."

The princess went over to her husband, kissed him, and was about to leave, but he held her back, embraced her, and — as tenderly as a young lover — kissed her several times, smiling. The two old people were briefly muddled and seemed unsure whether it was they who were in love again or their daughter. Once they had gone, Levin went up to his fiancée and took her hand. He was composed now and could speak, and there was a great deal he wanted to tell her. But what came out wasn't what he had meant to say at all.
"How I knew it would turn out this way! I never let myself hope for it, and yet inside I was always certain," he said. "I believe it was meant to be."

"And so did I!" she said. "Even when...." She stopped, then went on, looking at him steadily with her honest eyes, "Even when I pushed my own happiness away. I always loved only you, but I got carried away. I have to tell you.... Can you forgive that?"
"Maybe it was for the best. You'll have so much of mine to forgive. I have to tell you...."

This was one of the things he had been meaning to bring up. He had decided from the start to tell her two things — that he wasn't pure as she was, and that he wasn't a believer. It was agonizing, but he felt he owed her both admissions.
"No, not now — later!" he said.
"All right, later, but you must tell me. I'm not afraid of anything. I want to know everything. Now it's settled."
He added: "Settled that you'll take me whatever I turn out to be — that you won't give me up? Yes?"
"Yes, yes."

Their conversation was broken off by Mademoiselle Linon, who came in with a put-on but tender smile to congratulate her favorite pupil. Before she had gone, the servants arrived with their congratulations. Then relatives turned up, and there began the state of blissful confusion that Levin did not emerge from until the day after the wedding. He felt constantly awkward and uncomfortable, but the intensity of his happiness kept on growing. He sensed that a great deal was being expected of him — what exactly, he couldn't say; he did everything he was told, and all of it made him happy. He had imagined his engagement would be unlike anyone else's, that the ordinary trappings would cheapen his unique happiness; but in the end he did exactly what everyone else did, and his happiness only grew from it, becoming more and more particular, more and more unlike anything that had ever happened before.
"Now we'll need sweets," Mademoiselle Linon announced — and off Levin drove to buy sweets.
"Well, I'm delighted," said Sviazhsky. "I'd recommend getting the bouquets from Fomin's."
"Oh — are bouquets needed?" And he drove off to Fomin's.
His brother offered to lend him money, since there'd be so many expenses, presents to be given....
"Oh — are presents needed?" And he hurried off to Foulde's.

And at the confectioner's, and at Fomin's, and at Foulde's, he saw that he was expected; that they were pleased to see him and took pride in his happiness, just like everyone else he encountered in those days. What was extraordinary was that not only did everyone like him, but even people who had previously been unsympathetic, cold, indifferent, were now enthusiastic about him, gave way to him in everything, handled his feelings with tenderness and tact, and shared his conviction that he was the happiest man in the world because his fiancée was beyond perfection. Kitty felt the same. When Countess Nordston hinted that she had hoped for something better, Kitty grew so indignant and argued so convincingly that nothing in the world could be better than Levin, that Countess Nordston was forced to concede the point, and never met him in Kitty's company again without a smile of rapturous admiration.

The confession he had promised her was the one painful episode of this time. He consulted the old prince, and with his approval gave Kitty the diary in which he had written down the confession that tormented him. He had kept this diary at the time precisely with a future wife in mind. Two things gave him anguish: his lack of purity and his lack of faith. The confession of unbelief passed without remark. She was religious, had never questioned the truths of religion, but his outward unbelief didn't trouble her at all. Through love she knew his whole soul, and in his soul she saw what she wanted, and the fact that such a soul might be called unbelieving meant nothing to her. The other confession set her weeping bitterly.

It was not without inner struggle that Levin handed her the diary. He knew that there couldn't and shouldn't be secrets between them, and so he had decided that this was how it had to be. But he hadn't grasped the effect it would have on her — he hadn't put himself in her place. It was only that same evening, when he came over before the theater, went into her room and saw her tear-streaked, pitiful, sweet face, miserable with a pain he had caused and could never undo, that he felt the abyss between his shameful past and her dovelike purity, and was horrified at what he had done.

"Take them — take these dreadful books away!" she said, pushing the notebooks aside on the table. "Why did you give them to me? No — it was better this way, all the same," she added, moved by his despairing face. "But it's awful, awful!"
He bowed his head and said nothing. There was nothing he could say.
"You can't forgive me," he whispered.
"Yes — I forgive you; but it's terrible!"

But his happiness was so immense that this confession didn't shatter it; it only added another shade to it. She forgave him; but from then on he considered himself even less worthy of her, bowed lower in spirit than ever before her, and prized his undeserved happiness more highly than ever.
